explanations.explanation: The synagogues, friend. Verse 20 says Saul promptly began to proclaim Jesus there. He went where the community gathered and said it out loud. I need three practice runs and a cookie just to order at a drive-through.
A marketplace has a big crowd, so I see why it sounds right. But the text never puts Saul there. Acts 9:20 says he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues. And he did it promptly, no warm-up lap.

The city gates do show up in this story, just not here. Acts 9:24 says people watched them day and night. Saul's preaching in verse 20 happens in the synagogues. Right city, wrong spot, and an easy one to mix up.

explanations.answer: He is the Son of God
explanations.explanation: Those are Saul's words, and they're big ones: “He is the Son of God.” Saul wasn't just saying nice things about Jesus. He was saying who Jesus is. I'd say that's a pretty bold first sermon, wouldn't you?
A great prophet is a fine thing to say about somebody. But it's not what Saul says. Verse 20 has him declaring, “He is the Son of God.” That's a lot more than great, friend.
Wise teacher sounds safe, like a compliment you'd put on a card. Saul goes a lot further than that. Acts 9:20 has him declaring, “He is the Son of God.” That's who Jesus is, and Saul said it plainly.

Astounded is the word in verse 21. The people knew who Saul was, so hearing him preach Jesus knocked them sideways. They even start asking questions about it. I'd be asking questions too, and I'd be holding my hat.

The text never says the crowd was delighted. Verse 21 says all who heard him were astounded. Then they start asking whether this is the same man who came to take people as prisoners. That's a crowd with questions, not a crowd throwing a party.
Nobody in that room was unmoved, friend. Verse 21 says all who heard him were astounded. Astounded is about as far from unmoved as you can get. I'm betting nobody checked their watch.

It goes the other way. Verse 22 says Saul was empowered all the more. He didn't shrink back when the questions came. He kept going and confounded the Jews living in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Christ.

Right, because Saul doesn't go quiet. Acts 9:22 says he was empowered all the more. He confounded the Jews living in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Christ. When I get stared at, I forget my own name, so that's impressive.

explanations.answer: By proving that Jesus is the Christ
explanations.explanation: Verse 22 says he confounded them by proving that Jesus is the Christ. The text gives Saul's proving as the way he did it. The Jews living in Damascus had no comeback. I know that feeling, mostly from group chats.

explanations.answer: By showing the high priest's letters
explanations.explanation: Letters from the high priest were part of why Saul headed to Damascus. He had asked for them so he could bring believers back as prisoners (Acts 9:1-2). But in verse 22 nobody pulls out a letter. Saul confounds them by proving that Jesus is the Christ.

explanations.answer: By performing a sign in the street
explanations.explanation: A sign in the street would make a great scene, but the text doesn't show one. Verse 22 says Saul confounded the Jews living in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Christ. His proving is what stopped them cold. No fireworks, just a man who was empowered all the more.
True. Verse 24 says Saul learned of their plot. He knew people were out to kill him. That's a heavy thing to know, and I think it must have weighed on him.

Saul wasn't left in the dark on this one. Acts 9:24 says plainly that Saul learned of their plot. He knew the Jews had conspired to kill him. It's a heavy part of the story, and I think it was a heavy thing to find out.

explanations.answer: In a basket through a window
explanations.explanation: His disciples took him and lowered him in a basket through a window in the wall, and they did it one night. With the gates watched day and night, a window was the way out. I've been stuck in some tight spots myself, but nobody ever lowered me out of one in a basket.

A cart would have to roll through a gate, and the gates were being watched day and night. Verse 25 has a different way out. His disciples took Saul and lowered him in a basket through a window in the wall. Nobody had to cross the watched gates.

No costume party in this story, friend. Verse 25 says his disciples took him and lowered him in a basket through a window in the wall. It happened one night, while the gates were being watched. Saul went out through the wall, not past the guards.

explanations.answer: They are all afraid of him
explanations.explanation: Verse 26 says they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple. I can't blame them for that, since his reputation got there before he did. Saul walked in with a long track record, and it wasn't the kind you want.
Nobody hands Saul a title on day one. Acts 9:26 says the disciples were all afraid of him. They didn't believe he was a disciple. That's a long way from putting him in charge.
A warm welcome would be nice, but that isn't what happens. Verse 26 says they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple. It takes another man to turn that room around.

The apostles, friend. Verse 27 says Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus (Acts 4:36), brought Saul to them. Then Barnabas told them how Saul had seen the Lord. That's one man putting his own name on the line for another.

Priests are in this story, just not here. In Damascus, the chief priests were who Saul came to hand people over to (Acts 9:21). In Jerusalem, Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus (Acts 4:36), brings him to the apostles.

The Pharisees don't show up anywhere in these verses. Acts 9:27 says Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus (Acts 4:36), brought Saul to the apostles. They're the ones who hear how Saul saw the Lord on the road. Good guess for a Jerusalem story, but the text names the apostles.

explanations.answer: How he spoke boldly in Damascus
explanations.explanation: Verse 27 says Barnabas described how Saul had spoken boldly in that city in the name of Jesus. So the apostles heard about the road and about Damascus. Barnabas gave them what he knew, and I think that's what changed the room.

explanations.answer: How he healed a blind man
explanations.explanation: No healing is mentioned here. Barnabas tells the apostles two things in verse 27. Saul had seen the Lord on the road to Damascus, and he had spoken boldly in that city in the name of Jesus.

explanations.answer: How he fasted for forty days
explanations.explanation: Forty days of fasting isn't in this passage. Verse 27 says Barnabas described how Saul had seen the Lord on the road. He also told them how Saul had spoken boldly in Damascus in the name of Jesus. Those two things made up his whole case.
True. Verse 29 says Saul talked and debated with the Grecian Jews, but they tried to kill him. That's a heavy turn after the good news of verse 28. Friend, that's some debate.

They did try. Acts 9:29 says Saul talked and debated with the Grecian Jews, but they tried to kill him. It's a heavy moment, and it comes right after Saul was moving about freely. I think that's a hard thing to read twice.
Tarsus is the one. Verse 30 says the brothers took Saul down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. His friends looked out for him. I think they cared about keeping him safe.
Antioch is a real city in the book of Acts, but it isn't in this verse. Acts 9:30 says the brothers took Saul down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. That's where the text sends him.
Joppa is another city in Acts, but not this time. Verse 30 says the brothers took Saul down to Caesarea. From there they sent him off to Tarsus. That's the only destination the text gives.

Verse 31 says the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria experienced a time of peace. It grew in strength and numbers. It lived in the fear of the Lord and the encouragement of the Holy Spirit. And that's the end of this passage. But this story isn't over, friend.

No famine here. Acts 9:31 says the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria experienced a time of peace. It was growing in strength and numbers, living in the fear of the Lord and the encouragement of the Holy Spirit. And this story isn't over, friend.

After the plots and the basket, mourning might feel like the next chapter. But verse 31 says the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria experienced a time of peace. It grew in strength and numbers, with the encouragement of the Holy Spirit. And this story isn't over, friend.
